      "text": "Here is the comprehensive Obsidian-optimized note file.\n\nI have reconstructed the missing **Binary Acids** section to bridge the gap before the lecture recording starts, ensuring a seamless flow into **Ternary Acids** and **Chemical Kinetics**.\n\n***\n\n# [[Inorganic Chemistry]]: Acids, Bases, and Introduction to Kinetics\n\n## 1. [[Binary Acids]] (Contextual Reconstruction)\n\u003e **Note to Self:** I missed the start of the lecture. Based on the transition into ternary acids, the lecturer covered binary acids ($HX$) immediately prior. Here is the reconstructed logic required to understand the subsequent topics.\n\n### General Structure\n*   **Formula:** $H_n X$ (where X is a non-metal, e.g., $HCl, H_2S$).\n*   **Dissociation:** $$HX_{(aq)} \\rightleftharpoons H^+_{(aq)} + X^-_{(aq)}$$\n\n### Trends in Acidity\nThe strength of a binary acid depends on two competing factors:\n1.  **Bond Polarity (Period Trend):** As electronegativity of $X$ increases (left to right), the $H-X$ bond becomes more polar, making $H^+$ easier to remove.\n    *   *Trend:* Acidity increases across a period.\n    *   *Example:* $CH_4 \u003c NH_3 \u003c H_2O \u003c HF$.\n2.  **Bond Strength (Group Trend):** As the size of $X$ increases (down a group), the $H-X$ bond becomes longer and weaker. **This is the dominant factor.**\n    *   *Trend:* Acidity increases down a group.\n    *   *Example:* $HF \\ll HCl \u003c HBr \u003c HI$.\n\n\u003e **Critical Analysis:** Unlike ternary acids (where electronegativity rules), in binary acids, **bond strength** is the primary driver for acidity down a group. $HI$ is the strongest because the bond is the weakest.\n\n---\n\n## 2. [[Ternary Acids]] (Oxoacids)\n\n### Structural Definition\n*   **Structure:** Contains Hydrogen, Oxygen, and a Central Atom ($Z$).\n*   **General Formula:** $H-O-Z$ (or $H_mZO_n$).\n*   **Key Concept:** The acidic proton is *always* bound to an Oxygen atom, forming a hydroxyl group ($-OH$) attached to the central atom.\n\n### Factors Affecting Acidity Strength\nThe strength depends on how easily the $O-H$ bond breaks to release $H^+$. This is determined by the **Inductive Effect**.\n\n#### 1. Electronegativity of the Central Atom ($Z$)\n*   If $Z$ is highly electronegative, it pulls electron density from the $O$ atom.\n*   The $O$ atom, in turn, pulls electron density from the $H$ atom.\n*   **Result:** The $O-H$ bond weakens (becomes more polar), and $H^+$ dissociates more easily.\n*   **Comparison:**\n    $$HOCl \u003c HOBr \u003c HOI$$\n    *   *Correction/Warning:* The transcript notes that $Cl$ is more electronegative than $I$. Therefore, the pull is stronger in $HOCl$.\n    *   **Trend:** Higher electronegativity of $Z \\rightarrow$ Stronger Acid.\n\n#### 2. Oxidation Number (Number of Oxygen Atoms)\n*   As the number of terminal Oxygen atoms (O atoms *not* bonded to H) increases, the electron density is pulled away from the central atom ($Z$) and the $O-H$ bond.\n*   **Delocalization:** The negative charge on the resulting anion (conjugate base) is stabilized by resonance over more oxygen atoms.\n*   **General Formula:** $O_nZ(OH)_m$. As $n$ increases, acidity increases.\n\n**Example: Chlorine Series**\n$$HClO \u003c HClO_2 \u003c HClO_3 \u003c HClO_4$$\n*   **Hypochlorous acid ($HClO$):** $+1$ oxidation state. Weakest.\n*   **Perchloric acid ($HClO_4$):** $+7$ oxidation state. Strongest.\n\n**Example: Nitrogen Series**\n*   **Nitrous Acid ($HNO_2$):** Weak acid.\n*   **Nitric Acid ($HNO_3$):** Strong acid.\n*   *Reasoning:* Nitrogen in $HNO_3$ has a higher oxidation state ($+5$) and more oxygen atoms to stabilize the anion via resonance.\n\n**Example: Sulfur Series**\n*   **Sulfurous Acid ($H_2SO_3$):** Weaker.\n*   **Sulfuric Acid ($H_2SO_4$):** Stronger ($+6$ oxidation state).\n\n---\n\n## 3. [[Phosphorus Acid Exceptions]]\n\u003e **Warning:** Phosphorus acids **do not** follow the standard rule that \"more Oxygens \u003d stronger acid\" in a straightforward way, nor does the formula $H_3...$ imply triprotic behavior. We must look at the physical structure.\n\n### The Structure Anomaly\nAcidity is determined by protons on **Oxygen** ($P-O-H$), not protons directly on **Phosphorus** ($P-H$). The $P-H$ bond is non-polar and does not dissociate.\n\n| Acid Name | Formula | Structure (SMILES) | Protic Nature | Strength (Notes*) |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| **Hypophosphorous** | $H_3PO_2$ | `[H]OP(\u003dO)([H])[H]` | **Monoprotic** (1 OH) | Strongest |\n| **Phosphorous** | $H_3PO_3$ | `[H]OP(\u003dO)(O[H])[H]` | **Diprotic** (2 OH) | Medium |\n| **Phosphoric** | $H_3PO_4$ | `[H]OP(\u003dO)(O[H])O[H]` | **Triprotic** (3 OH) | Weakest |\n\n### Justification of Strength Inversion ($H_3PO_2 \u003e H_3PO_3 \u003e H_3PO_4$)\n*   **The Lecture Logic:** The lecturer argues that despite having fewer oxygens, $H_3PO_2$ is stronger due to the specific structural arrangement and the inductive effect (or lack of opposing resonance stabilization relative to the proton release).\n*   *Note:* Standard literature often lists $pK_a$ values as very similar ($2.1$, $1.3$, $2.0$), but for this course, memorize the **Inverse Order** provided in the notes (Page 1 bottom).\n\n---\n\n## 4. Special Cases: [[Boric Acid]] and Salts\n\n### Boric Acid ($H_3BO_3$)\n*   **Behavior:** It is **not** a Brønsted-Lowry acid (doesn\u0027t donate its own proton directly). It acts as a **Lewis Acid**.\n*   **Mechanism:** The Boron atom is electron-deficient (sextet). It accepts an electron pair from a water molecule\u0027s hydroxide ion ($OH^-$).\n*   **Reaction:**\n    $$B(OH)_3 + 2H_2O \\rightleftharpoons [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+$$\n*   **Result:** It effectively releases a proton from the *water*, not the boron structure itself.\n\n### Hydrolysis of Salts (Brief Overview)\nThe acidity of a salt depends on the strength of the parent acid/base.\n*   **$Na_3PO_4$:** Salt of Strong Base ($NaOH$) + Weak Acid ($HPO_4^{2-}$ conjugate). **Solution is Basic.**\n*   **$NaH_2PO_4$:** Amphoteric, but generally acidic due to the ionization of the remaining protons.\n\n---\n\n## 5. [[Chemical Kinetics]]\n\n### 5.1 Kinetics vs. Thermodynamics\n*   **[[Thermodynamics]]:** Determines **IF** a reaction can occur (Spontaneity).\n    *   Condition: $\\Delta G \u003c 0$.\n    *   *Example:* $2NO + O_2 \\rightarrow 2NO_2$ (Spontaneous at $25^\\circ C$, $\\Delta G \u003d -140 kJ$).\n*   **[[Kinetics]]:** Determines **HOW FAST** a reaction occurs (Rate).\n    *   *Example:* $2H_2 + O_2 \\rightarrow 2H_2O$.\n    *   Thermodynamically favorable ($\\Delta G \\ll 0$), but kinetically **extremely slow** at room temperature without a catalyst (spark).\n\n### 5.2 Factors Affecting Reaction Rate\n1.  **Physical State:** Surface area of solid reactants. (Finely ground powder reacts faster than chunks).\n2.  **Concentration:** Higher concentration \u003d more collisions.\n3.  **Temperature:** Higher T \u003d particles have more Kinetic Energy $\\rightarrow$ more successful collisions (Activation Energy).\n4.  **Catalyst:** Lowers Activation Energy ($E_a$).\n\n### 5.3 Reaction Rate Definition\nThe change in concentration of a reactant or product over time.\n$$v \u003d \\pm \\frac{dc}{dt}$$\n*   *(Negative sign for reactants consuming, positive for products forming).*\n\n### 5.4 The Rate Law\nThe mathematical relationship between rate and concentration.\n$$v \u003d k \\cdot [A]^\\alpha \\cdot [B]^\\beta$$\n*   $k$: Rate constant (temperature dependent).\n*   $[A], [B]$: Concentrations of reactants.\n*   $\\alpha, \\beta$: **Orders of reaction**.\n    *   **Crucial Note:** $\\alpha$ and $\\beta$ are determined **experimentally**. They are NOT necessarily the stoichiometric coefficients ($a, b$) from the balanced equation ($aA + bB \\rightarrow Products$).\n\n### 5.5 Collision Theory (Teorija Trkov)\n*   **Basic Premise:** For a reaction to occur, particles must collide.\n*   **Success Factors:**\n    1.  **Correct Orientation:** Steric factor.\n    2.  **Sufficient Energy:** Must exceed Activation Energy ($E_a$).\n\n***\n\n### **General Formulas \u0026 Constants**\n*   **Dissociation of base:** $MOH \\rightleftharpoons M^+ + OH^-$\n*   **General Rate Law:** $v \u003d k[A]^\\alpha[B]^\\beta$\n*   **Arrhenius Equation (implied by T dependence):** $k \u003d A \\cdot e^{-E_a/RT}$",

        "text": " breaks to release $H^+$. This is determined by the **Inductive Effect**.\n\n#### 1. Electronegativity of"
      }, {
        "text": " the Central Atom ($Z$)\n*   If $Z$ is highly electronegative, it pulls electron density from the $O$"
      }, {
        "text": " atom.\n*   The $O$ atom, in turn, pulls electron density from the $H$ atom.\n*"
      }, {
        "text": "   **Result:** The $O-H$ bond weakens (becomes more polar), and $H^+$ dissociates more"
      }, {
        "text": " easily.\n*   **Comparison:**\n    $$HOCl \u003c HOBr \u003c HOI$$\n    *   "
      }, {
        "text": "*Correction/Warning:* The transcript notes that $Cl$ is more electronegative than $I$. Therefore, the pull"
      }, {
        "text": " is stronger in $HOCl$.\n    *   **Trend:** Higher electronegativity of $Z \\rightarrow$ Stronger"
      }, {
        "text": " Acid.\n\n#### 2. Oxidation Number (Number of Oxygen Atoms)\n*   As the number of terminal Oxygen atoms"
      }, {
        "text": " (O atoms *not* bonded to H) increases, the electron density is pulled away from the central atom ($Z$) and the"
      }, {
        "text": " $O-H$ bond.\n*   **Delocalization:** The negative charge on the resulting anion (conjugate base)"
      }, {
        "text": " is stabilized by resonance over more oxygen atoms.\n*   **General Formula:** $O_nZ(OH)_m"
      }, {
        "text": "$. As $n$ increases, acidity increases.\n\n**Example: Chlorine Series**\n$$HClO \u003c HClO"
      }, {
        "text": "_2 \u003c HClO_3 \u003c HClO_4$$\n*   **Hypochlorous acid ($HClO"
      }, {
        "text": "$):** $+1$ oxidation state. Weakest.\n*   **Perchloric acid ($HClO_4"
      }, {
        "text": "$):** $+7$ oxidation state. Strongest.\n\n**Example: Nitrogen Series**\n*   **Nitrous"
      }, {
        "text": " Acid ($HNO_2$):** Weak acid.\n*   **Nitric Acid ($HNO_3$):"
      }, {
        "text": "** Strong acid.\n*   *Reasoning:* Nitrogen in $HNO_3$ has a higher oxidation state ($+"
      }, {
        "text": "5$) and more oxygen atoms to stabilize the anion via resonance.\n\n**Example: Sulfur Series**\n*   **Sulfurous Acid"
      }, {
        "text": " ($H_2SO_3$):** Weaker.\n*   **Sulfuric Acid ($H_2SO_4"
      }, {
        "text": "$):** Stronger ($+6$ oxidation state).\n\n---\n\n## 3. [[Phosphorus Acid Exceptions]]\n\u003e"
      }, {
        "text": " **Warning:** Phosphorus acids **do not** follow the standard rule that \"more Oxygens \u003d stronger acid\" in a"
      }, {
        "text": " straightforward way, nor does the formula $H_3...$ imply triprotic behavior. We must look at the"
      }, {
        "text": " physical structure.\n\n### The Structure Anomaly\nAcidity is determined by protons on **Oxygen** ($P-O-H"
      }, {
        "text": "$), not protons directly on **Phosphorus** ($P-H$). The $P-H$ bond is non-polar and does"
      }, {
        "text": " not dissociate.\n\n| Acid Name | Formula | Structure (SMILES) | Protic Nature | Strength (Notes*)"
      }, {
        "text": " |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| **Hypophosphorous** |"
      }, {
        "text": " $H_3PO_2$ | `[H]OP(\u003dO)([H])[H]` | **Monoprotic**"
      }, {
        "text": " (1 OH) | Strongest |\n| **Phosphorous** | $H_3PO_3$ | `["
      }, {
        "text": "H]OP(\u003dO)(O[H])[H]` | **Diprotic** (2 OH) | Medium |\n| **"
      }, {
        "text": "Phosphoric** | $H_3PO_4$ | `[H]OP(\u003dO)(O[H"
      }, {
        "text": "])O[H]` | **Triprotic** (3 OH) | Weakest |\n\n### Justification of Strength In"
      }, {
        "text": "version ($H_3PO_2 \u003e H_3PO_3 \u003e H_3PO_4$)\n"
      }, {
        "text": "*   **The Lecture Logic:** The lecturer argues that despite having fewer oxygens, $H_3PO_2$ is stronger"
      }, {
        "text": " due to the specific structural arrangement and the inductive effect (or lack of opposing resonance stabilization relative to the proton release).\n*   "
      }, {
        "text": "*Note:* Standard literature often lists $pK_a$ values as very similar ($2.1$, $1.3$,"
      }, {
        "text": " $2.0$), but for this course, memorize the **Inverse Order** provided in the notes (Page 1 bottom"
      }, {
        "text": ").\n\n---\n\n## 4. Special Cases: [[Boric Acid]] and Salts\n\n### Boric Acid ($H"
      }, {
        "text": "_3BO_3$)\n*   **Behavior:** It is **not** a Brønsted-Lowry acid"
      }, {
        "text": " (doesn\u0027t donate its own proton directly). It acts as a **Lewis Acid**.\n*   **Mechanism:** The"
      }, {
        "text": " Boron atom is electron-deficient (sextet). It accepts an electron pair from a water molecule\u0027s hydroxide ion ($"
      }, {
        "text": "OH^-$).\n*   **Reaction:**\n    $$B(OH)_3 + 2H_2"
      }, {
        "text": "O \\rightleftharpoons [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+$$\n*   **Result:** It effectively"
      }, {
        "text": " releases a proton from the *water*, not the boron structure itself.\n\n### Hydrolysis of Salts (Brief Overview)\nThe"
      }, {
        "text": " acidity of a salt depends on the strength of the parent acid/base.\n*   **$Na_3PO_4$"
      }, {
        "text": ":** Salt of Strong Base ($NaOH$) + Weak Acid ($HPO_4^{2-}$ conjugate). **Solution is Basic.**\n"
      }, {
        "text": "*   **$NaH_2PO_4$:** Amphoteric, but generally acidic due to the ionization of the remaining"
      }, {
        "text": " protons.\n\n---\n\n## 5. [[Chemical Kinetics]]\n\n### 5.1 Kinetics vs. Thermodynamics\n"
      }, {
        "text": "*   **[[Thermodynamics]]:** Determines **IF** a reaction can occur (Spontaneity).\n    *   Condition"
      }, {
        "text": ": $\\Delta G \u003c 0$.\n    *   *Example:* $2NO + O_2 \\rightarrow"
      }, {
        "text": " 2NO_2$ (Spontaneous at $25^\\circ C$, $\\Delta G \u003d -140 kJ$)."
      }, {
        "text": "\n*   **[[Kinetics]]:** Determines **HOW FAST** a reaction occurs (Rate).\n    *   *Example"
      }, {
        "text": ":* $2H_2 + O_2 \\rightarrow 2H_2O$.\n    *   Ther"
      }, {
        "text": "modynamically favorable ($\\Delta G \\ll 0$), but kinetically **extremely slow** at room temperature without a catalyst ("
      }, {
        "text": "spark).\n\n### 5.2 Factors Affecting Reaction Rate\n1.  **Physical State:** Surface area of solid"
      }, {
        "text": " reactants. (Finely ground powder reacts faster than chunks).\n2.  **Concentration:** Higher concentration \u003d more collisions."
      }, {
        "text": "\n3.  **Temperature:** Higher T \u003d particles have more Kinetic Energy $\\rightarrow$ more successful collisions (Activation Energy).\n"
      }, {
        "text": "4.  **Catalyst:** Lowers Activation Energy ($E_a$).\n\n### 5.3 Reaction Rate Definition"
      }, {
        "text": "\nThe change in concentration of a reactant or product over time.\n$$v \u003d \\pm \\frac{dc}{dt}$$\n"
      }, {
        "text": "*   *(Negative sign for reactants consuming, positive for products forming).*\n\n### 5.4 The Rate Law\n"
      }, {
        "text": "The mathematical relationship between rate and concentration.\n$$v \u003d k \\cdot [A]^\\alpha \\cdot [B]^\\"
      }, {
        "text": "beta$$\n*   $k$: Rate constant (temperature dependent).\n*   $[A], [B]$:"
      }, {
        "text": " Concentrations of reactants.\n*   $\\alpha, \\beta$: **Orders of reaction**.\n    *   **Crucial Note"
      }, {
        "text": ":** $\\alpha$ and $\\beta$ are determined **experimentally**. They are NOT necessarily the stoichiometric coefficients ($a, b$)"
      }, {
        "text": " from the balanced equation ($aA + bB \\rightarrow Products$).\n\n### 5.5 Collision Theory (Teor"
      }, {
        "text": "ija Trkov)\n*   **Basic Premise:** For a reaction to occur, particles must collide.\n*   **"
      }, {
        "text": "Success Factors:**\n    1.  **Correct Orientation:** Steric factor.\n    2.  **Sufficient Energy"
      }, {
        "text": ":** Must exceed Activation Energy ($E_a$).\n\n***\n\n### **General Formulas \u0026 Constants**\n*   **Diss"
      }, {
        "text": "ociation of base:** $MOH \\rightleftharpoons M^+ + OH^-$\n*   **General Rate Law:** $v"
      }, {
        "text": " \u003d k[A]^\\alpha[B]^\\beta$\n*   **Arrhenius Equation (implied by"
      }, {
        "text": " T dependence):** $k \u003d A \\cdot e^{-E_a/RT}$"
      }, {

      }]
